implementation_notes: Java has no ring buffer in the JDK, and the concurrency story is that ArrayBlockingQueue is the general bounded queue (lock-based, FIFO, fixed capacity) and Disruptor is the high-performance ring for multiple producers and consumers. For a hand-written SPSC ring, the indices are AtomicLong (or VarHandle long fields) with the acquire/release pattern, padded via inheritance or @Contended (with -XX:-RestrictContended for application classes). ArrayDeque is a growable circular array and is the answer for a single-threaded ring that can resize; PriorityBlockingQueue is for priority. The choice: ArrayDeque for a single-threaded ring that may need to grow, ArrayBlockingQueue for a bounded blocking MPMC queue, and a hand-written SPSC ring (or Disruptor) for a measured high-throughput path. As in every managed language, the JIT can eliminate much of the overhead, so measure before hand-rolling.
idiom_name: ArrayDeque (single-threaded, growable) / ArrayBlockingQueue (bounded, blocking) / hand-written SPSC ring with padded VarHandle indices
pitfalls: ArrayDeque is not thread-safe; ArrayBlockingQueue is bounded and blocking but takes a lock on every operation, which is the contention the ring avoids.
AtomicLong.lazySet is a release store and get() is a full volatile read - mixing them up (e.g. lazySet for a read) breaks the ordering.
The head and tail AtomicLongs are separate objects and may share a cache line; for a real SPSC ring pad them (inheritance or -XX:-RestrictContended @Contended).
On a 32-bit JVM, a long field is not atomic - use AtomicLong or ensure 64-bit atomics (the same caveat as the atomics pattern).
